html:
The oldest of the Vedas: a collection of 1,028 hymns in Vedic Sanskrit, composed in the Punjab between about 1500 and 1200 BCE. It is one of the oldest texts in any Indo-European language and one of the four sacred texts at the root of Hinduism.

The hymns are arranged in ten books. Books 2 to 7, the "family books", are the oldest; each belongs to one family of priest-poets. They praise gods such as Indra, the warrior who kills the serpent and frees the waters; Agni, the fire who carries offerings to heaven; and Soma, a sacred drink. Book 10 is later and includes the hymn of the cosmic man, which names the four varnas, and the creation hymn that ends by wondering whether even the highest god knows how the world began.

The hymns give a picture of the early Vedic period: cattle herding, horses, chariots, tribal wars, and the land of seven rivers. Book 7 tells of a Battle of Ten Kings. Their language is very close to that of the Iranian Avesta, a sign of the shared roots described under Indo-Aryan migrations.

The most striking thing about the Rigveda is how it survived. For some 3,000 years priests passed it on by memory, using methods of recitation that repeat each word in several patterns so that errors are caught. The oral text is believed to have changed remarkably little. The oldest surviving manuscripts are only about a thousand years old. Later Vedic thought, including the Upanishads, built on it.
